pages.text: The bus bumped along a red road north of Techiman. “Welcome to Bono Manso,” said Mr Sarpong. “This quiet place was once a busy capital. Today we look for clues about it, and I want you to question everything, even the signs.” Akwasi raised an eyebrow. Josephine opened her notebook.

“Welcome to Bono Manso,” said Mr Sarpong.
“This quiet place was once a busy capital.
Today we look for clues about it, and I want you to question everything, even the signs.” Akwasi raised an eyebrow.
Josephine opened her notebook.
pages.alt: A school bus on a red road passes savanna-forest toward a quiet village.

pages.text: Mr Sarpong knelt by a trench. “Archaeologists date the founding of this town to about the year 1000,” he said. “They also found older traces in nearby rock shelters, about six hundred years earlier. Local tradition and archaeology together suggest that the people of Manso descended from the early Akan who lived there.”

“Archaeologists date the founding of this town to about the year 1000,” he said.

Local tradition and archaeology together suggest that the people of Manso descended from the early Akan who lived there.”
pages.alt: A teacher kneels by a neat trench in the ground where pottery is showing.

pages.text: “Manso was the capital of the Bono state,” said Mr Sarpong, “from the eleventh century until 1723. By the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries it was an important centre of trade and ritual. People often call Bono the earliest of the Akan states, but that is a claim we should always check against more than one source.”

pages.alt: A map of the Bono state with a town in the middle and roads running outward.

pages.text: “Why was it so busy?” asked Josephine. “Gold,” said Mr Sarpong. “The Akan goldfields lay to the south. Traders carried the gold north, along with kola nuts, and brought back salt, leather and cloth. Merchants called Juula, many of them Muslims, were part of this trade. The road reached markets such as Djenné and Timbuktu, far away in the Sahel.”

pages.text: “There was a large market called Dwabirem, to the southwest,” said Mr Sarpong. “It brought together people from the forest and the savanna. It is a good reminder that Ghana’s history is not only about the coast. Long before ships came, trade roads linked the interior to the Sahara and beyond.”

pages.text: “In 1723, Opoku Ware I of the Asante destroyed Bono Manso,” said Mr Sarpong. “After that, the town of Techiman became the regional centre. Techiman remained under Asante until the late nineteenth century.” Akwasi was quiet for a moment. “So a whole capital can disappear in a single year,” he said. “And its story is still here,” said Mr Sarpong, “in the soil and in memory.”

pages.text: At the village entrance, they read a faded sign. “It says Manso was a major slave market for the Atlantic trade,” said Josephine. Mr Sarpong frowned. “Careful,” he said. “Some tourism signs say that. But historians who have studied the evidence say there is no proof that Manso was a major market for the Atlantic slave trade. It may have played a small part in local trade. When a sign makes a big claim, ask: where is the evidence?”

pages.alt: Two pupils read a worn signpost while the teacher shakes his head slowly.

pages.text: On the bus back, Akwasi counted on his fingers. “If it was founded about the year 1000, it is about a thousand years since then. That is a very long time.” “And it is still teaching us,” said Josephine. Mr Sarpong smiled. “Then you are already doing what archaeologists do,” he said. “You are asking, checking, and writing down what you do not yet know.” The end.
